pge.small: Likely range: $35 owed to $38 owed. This is the year's grid fees minus the minimum charges already paid. The Oct 1 bill already shows $33.76; about $3 more in fees through Oct 26 would make it about $37.

vce.small: As a bill credit. Likely range: $88 credited to $10 credited.

why_pge: This home's solar sent more energy to the grid than the home pulled from it, so its energy account ends the year about $321 in credit. That leftover dollar credit is wiped out at the true-up. PG&E pays nothing for it, because for Valley Clean Energy customers the payment for extra energy comes from VCE (see below).

There's a small fee on every kWh pulled from the grid that solar credits can't cancel (PG&E calls it the "non-bypassable charge"). It adds up all year and is settled at the true-up: about $86.77 this year. Most of it came in Nov–Feb, when the home used the most grid power.

The monthly minimum charge paid Nov–Feb ($50.40) counts against those fees. What's left, $36.37, is the true-up bill. The Oct 1 bill already shows this: "YTD Estimated NEM Charges At True-Up $33.76" ($84.17 of fees minus $50.41 of minimum charges), and one more billing cycle of fees (to Oct 26) will be added.
The 2025 true-up worked the same way. The fees ($141) were less than the minimum charges already paid ($146.50), so $0 was owed.

The monthly bill is just the fixed ~$24/month Base Services Charge (about $190 this year), which solar credits can't reduce. Three state Climate Credits ($46.26 on the May 4 bill, $36.18 on the Sep 2 bill and $36.18 on the Oct 1 bill) offset part of it. All-in, PG&E costs this home about $205 for the year.
why_vce: Valley Clean Energy (VCE) is the local public agency that supplies this home's electricity. PG&E still delivers it and sends the bill. VCE's side runs on its own year, March through February.
Summer solar builds up VCE credit, and that credit pays for winter use as it comes up, so nothing is owed to VCE month to month.
In February VCE pays for the extra kWh the home sent to the grid over the year: 1,255 kWh × 3.9¢ (wholesale price about 2.9¢ plus VCE's 1¢ bonus) = $49, as a bill credit.
The remaining dollar credit (about $111) is not paid out. The payout counts kWh, not dollars.
The range depends on how much grid power the home uses this winter (EV charging adds to it).
leftover: Leftover dollar credits: forfeited at both PG&E and VCE. They are never paid out at the full retail value.

Extra kWh (more exported than used): paid only by VCE, once a year in February, at the wholesale rate plus a 1¢ bonus (about 3.9¢/kWh). It arrives as a bill credit, or as a check if the account is closed.

PG&E pays nothing for extra kWh to customers of a local provider like VCE. Its tariff hands that job to VCE. The 2025 PG&E statement shows no surplus payment, even though the home exported about 1,497 kWh more than it used.

  • This home's imports are almost all "other hours" (in the Aug cycle only 0.2% came at 5–8 pm), so a kWh from the grid really costs about 33.8¢ in summer and 34.3¢ in winter.
  • An exported kWh earns the same as an imported one costs, except the 1.2¢ grid fee (never credited back), plus VCE's 1¢ bonus on each month's net exports. Those credits only cancel charges within the true-up year. Leftover credit is forfeited. The only cash is VCE's surplus payout of about 3.9¢ per net surplus kWh for the year.
  • What an extra kWh really means for this home this year: both balances end in forfeited credit, so an extra kWh from the grid costs only about 5.1¢ (grid fee + a smaller VCE payout). An extra kWh exported is worth about 3.9¢.
  • Compared with 2025, per-kWh prices are 16–21% lower in summer and 18–19% lower in winter, because PG&E moved costs into the fixed Base Services Charge: $24.12/month now vs a $12.26/month minimum in 2025.

assumptions: The home's PG&E 15-minute meter data (2024-10-01 to 2026-10-01) is used for every day it covers, with the actual 5–8 pm weekday peak (holidays excluded). This covers 93% of the current PG&E year and 60% of the current VCE year.

What the meter shows: through Feb 2026 the home pulled very little from the grid at 5–8 pm (under 3%). In Mar–Jul 2026 it was 7–14%, but on very small amounts, and it's back near 0% since August. Exports at 5–8 pm are about 1% most months, but 9–32% in Aug–Oct, when the Powerwall sends power out in the evening.

Days without meter data (before Oct 2024, and future months) use Tesla app totals, scaled up about 5% to match the PG&E meter, and split using the 5–8 pm shares the meter showed for that month. Future months are a weighted average of past years. The range is ±1 standard deviation of past usage. EV charging adds about 66 kWh/month.
PG&E's true-up year follows the account's billing cycle (last year: 10/25/2024–10/26/2025). This year is assumed to end Oct 26, 2026.

Grid fees (non-bypassable charges) build up all year and are settled at the true-up, with minimum charges already paid counted against them. The 2025 statement and the Oct 1, 2026 bill both show this ($84.17 of fees so far minus $50.41 of minimum charges = $33.76 estimated). The model gets $83.81 of fees for the same dates.

Rates: PG&E's published E-TOU-D rates for each date, and VCE's published generation rates. Future rates rise 4.8%/yr from 2027. The PG&E-side rate before Sep 2025 includes a correction of −1.3¢/kWh, fitted to the 2025 statement.
bill_verdict: Checked against 13 monthly PG&E bills (Oct 2025 – Oct 2026): the grid fee was never charged monthly. It shows up only in the NEM details, which settle at the true-up. The running total on the bills ($84.17 by Sep 24, 2026) equals the sum of the monthly lines, and nothing was charged twice.
